title: Methods
text:
Every indicator follows the same pipeline:

Download open data with a script in R/. Raw files stay local and are not committed to Git.
Check against a published figure wherever one exists, so errors in my processing would show up.
Summarise into a small tidy file in data/processed/.
Assess status, trend, and confidence, recorded in data/lookup/indicator_status.csv, which drives the report card.
Render with Quarto.

How status, trend, and confidence are assigned
These are my independent judgements, written down so they are transparent and repeatable. They are not official assessments.

title: Methods
text:
An epidemiologist’s lens
Several indicators borrow ideas from population health surveillance:

Before-after comparisons without a control group (seabirds): describe the size of change, and be explicit that this alone cannot establish cause.
Secular trends (seabirds, Gannet): a population that was growing before an outbreak makes a simple before-after comparison understate the impact.
Coverage as a response rate (seabirds): the share of the population surveyed affects how far a result generalises.
Counts are not populations (seals): haul-out counts are a consistent index, not a census of every animal.
Uncertainty reported alongside estimates (all): including when it is a minimum, as with Poisson intervals on large counts.

title: Seabirds after avian flu
text:
The short version

At the nine Scottish SPAs surveyed for Great Skua, breeding territories fell from 6,570 to 1,524 (-77%).
At six Scottish Northern Gannet SPAs, nest counts fell from 169,054 to 131,361 (-22%). Against a baseline projected forward for pre-outbreak growth, the fall is -28%.
Not every species declined everywhere. Guillemot counts, for example, rose at some SPAs and fell at others.
These are before-and-after counts at surveyed sites. They show a large drop that coincides with the outbreak, but on their own they cannot prove how much of it HPAI caused.

title: Seabirds after avian flu
text:
What this measures
The change in the number of breeding seabirds at Scottish Special Protection Areas (SPAs) between a pre-outbreak baseline (mostly from the Seabirds Count census, 2015 to 2021) and a coordinated survey in 2023, after highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI H5N1) caused mass seabird deaths in 2021 and 2022. Counts are of breeding units: apparently occupied nests, sites, or territories, or individual birds for Guillemot.

title: Seabirds after avian flu
text:
Why it matters
Scotland holds internationally important seabird populations, many protected by SPAs under the Habitats Regulations. HPAI arrived on top of existing declines: the Seabirds Count census found that most seabird species in Scotland had already declined since the previous census. Seabird abundance and breeding success are OSPAR and UK Marine Strategy indicators of marine bird status.

title: Seabirds after avian flu
section: Reading this like an outbreak investigation
text:
Reading this like an outbreak investigation


What the data can tell us

Magnitude: how much smaller breeding numbers were in 2023 at the sites surveyed.
Distribution: which species and which colonies changed most.
Timing: the drop coincides with the outbreak, and for some species it is far outside their recent trend.



What it cannot tell us on its own

Cause: there is no unexposed comparison group, so this is a before-after design. Other pressures were operating at the same time.
Mechanism: fewer breeding birds could mean deaths, or survivors skipping a breeding season.
The full picture: only surveyed sites are included, and mortality after early 2023 is not captured.



The epidemiological questions behind each chart:

Is the change real or noise? The forest plot shows each colony’s change with a confidence interval.
What would have happened anyway? For Gannet, the report projects each colony’s pre-outbreak trend forward to 2021. Comparing against that projection is like adjusting for a secular trend.
Who was counted? Coverage (the share of the population surveyed) works like a response rate, and it varies a lot between species.

title: Seabirds after avian flu
text:
Trend and status

UK picture: 13 species











Colony by colony: Great Skua and Gannet









The confidence intervals are narrow because these are large counts. That makes them a minimum estimate of uncertainty: they reflect counting noise only, not observer error, survey timing, or differences between baseline years. Even so, the Great Skua declines are far too large and too consistent to be explained by noise.


Gannet: how much depends on the baseline?









Gannet colonies were growing before the outbreak, and some baselines date from 2014. Comparing 2023 with the counted baseline gives -22%. Comparing it with each colony’s projected 2021 size gives -28%. This is the same logic as adjusting for a secular trend: if a population was rising, a simple before-after comparison understates the impact.

title: Seabirds after avian flu
text:
Confidence
Medium. The 2023 survey was large and coordinated, and for Great Skua, Gannet, and the terns it covered most of the population. But:

Baseline years vary (2014 to 2021), so some of each change happened before the outbreak.
A few 2023 counts are flagged by the report authors as preliminary or low confidence.
Coverage is low for some species, so totals may not represent the whole population.

title: Seabirds after avian flu
text:
Limitations

Attribution: the report’s authors consider HPAI the main driver for Great Skua, Gannet, and Roseate Tern, and likely for Sandwich and Common Tern. For species already in long-term decline, separating HPAI from other pressures is harder. This page reports change; it does not estimate a causal effect.
Breeding numbers only: the data do not include breeding success or adult survival.
Incomplete timing: further HPAI deaths in 2023 happened after these counts.
Transcription: SPA figures were transcribed from the report’s PDF tables (table and page recorded for each row) and checked against printed totals where available.

title: Seabirds after avian flu
text:
Optional next step
With approved access to the Seabird Monitoring Programme database (BTO/JNCC), annual counts at monitored colonies would show whether populations have started to recover since 2023, and allow a proper interrupted time-series analysis. Any such analysis would follow the SMP data use policy.

title: Wild Atlantic salmon
text:
What this measures
Each year the Scottish Government assesses the conservation status of 173 wild Atlantic salmon stocks: single rivers, or groups of rivers where catches cannot be separated. A stock’s status is the probability that it will meet its conservation limit (the number of spawning adults needed for a healthy population) over five years:

Good: at least an 80% probability. No extra management needed.
Moderate: a 60 to 80% probability. Catch-and-release strongly encouraged.
Poor: under a 60% probability. Mandatory catch-and-release for the season.

The grading for each season is based on the previous assessment, so the “2026” grading reflects the most recent data.

title: Wild Atlantic salmon
text:
Why it matters
Atlantic salmon is a protected species under the Habitats Regulations, with 17 Special Areas of Conservation designated for it in Scotland. It moves between rivers and the open ocean, so its status reflects conditions in both freshwater and the sea. This indicator reports status only. It does not try to attribute change to any one pressure.

title: Wild Atlantic salmon
text:
Trend and status
115 of 173 stocks (66%) were in poor conservation status for the 2026 season, up from 102 (59%) in 2021.










Where did stocks move?

title: Wild Atlantic salmon
text:
Confidence
High that the gradings are reported accurately, since they are the official assessments. Medium for reading a trend from them:

Six seasons is a short window.
Each grading already averages over five years, so successive seasons are not independent.
Stocks near a threshold can change category with small changes in the underlying probability.

title: Wild Atlantic salmon
text:
Limitations

Status is categorical. It hides how close a stock is to a boundary.
Assessments rely mainly on rod catch data (plus counters where available), which is affected by fishing effort and river conditions, not only by fish numbers.
8 fishery districts have no individual river data and are graded poor by default.
Some rivers take the lower grade of an overlapping SAC, so their grading may not reflect their own assessment.
Stock boundaries are not openly available, so the map shows river mouths rather than catchments.
National counts are the official published figures. River-level data, the transitions grid, and the map are my reconstruction from the published tables. That reconstruction gives 173 stocks and matches the official Good, Moderate, and Poor counts exactly for every season from 2021 to 2026. The check caught two quirks in the source tables: one stock (North Harris SAC) spans two fishery districts, and one row used a different dash in a grouped river name.

title: Report card
section: How to read this report card
text:
How to read this report card

Status summarises recent condition in plain language. It is my independent judgement from the published data, not an official assessment.
Trend describes direction of change over the period shown. Sea temperature is a context indicator, so it has no “good” or “bad” direction.
Confidence is reported separately so a clear trend in patchy data is not mistaken for a certain one.







This is an independent personal project. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by NatureScot, the Scottish Government Marine Directorate, JNCC, RSPB, BTO, or SMRU. For official assessments see Scotland’s Marine Assessment 2020.

title: About
text:
I’m Emma Branch, an epidemiologist and health data analyst (PhD candidate, Population and Public Health, UBC) with about ten years’ experience working with linked population data, R, and GIS.
I built this report card to learn about Scotland’s marine environment and its assessment frameworks, and to show how indicator reporting, spatial analysis, and honest communication of uncertainty transfer from population health to marine biodiversity. I am new to Scottish marine ecology, so I have aimed to describe what the data show without overclaiming.

title: Framework map
text: This table is the spine of the project. Each indicator is mapped to the reporting framework it would feed into. Links are my reading of the published documents and are marked as checked once I have confirmed them against the source text.

title: Framework map
text:
Frameworks in brief

Scottish Biodiversity Strategy to 2045: Scotland’s overarching biodiversity strategy (final version November 2024), with the first Delivery Plan covering 2024 to 2030. The Delivery Plan includes the “30 by 30” commitment and an action to develop marine biodiversity monitoring aligned with the UK Marine Strategy.
Natural Environment (Scotland) Act 2026: Part 1 creates a legally binding framework for statutory nature restoration targets, with monitoring and reporting duties. Royal Assent 12 March 2026.
Marine (Scotland) Act 2010: marine planning, Nature Conservation MPAs, and seal conservation in Scottish territorial waters.
Habitats Regulations: protection of SACs and SPAs (the UK site network, formerly part of Natura 2000).
UK Marine Strategy: Good Environmental Status assessed against 11 descriptors.
OSPAR: the North-East Atlantic regional convention. Common indicators include B1 (marine bird abundance), B3 (breeding success), M3 (seal abundance and distribution), and M5 (grey seal pup production). Latest assessment: Quality Status Report 2023.
Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework: 23 targets for 2030, including Target 3 (30x30).

Rows marked ✓ were confirmed against the source documents (November 2026). The salmon row has one OSPAR link still to confirm.

title: MPA coverage and 30x30
text:
What this measures
The share of Scotland’s seas that lies inside at least one designated Marine Protected Area (MPA). This includes Nature Conservation MPAs, Special Areas of Conservation (SACs), and Special Protection Areas (SPAs), inshore and offshore. Where sites overlap, the area is counted once.

title: MPA coverage and 30x30
text:
Why it matters
Target 3 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework asks countries to make sure that at least 30% of coastal and marine areas are effectively conserved and managed by 2030 (“30x30”). The word effectively matters. Designation is the first step. The target is about protection that works in practice, through management measures, monitoring, and enforcement.

title: MPA coverage and 30x30
text:
Trend and status
36.9% of Scottish seas (229,228 km² of 621,789 km²) is inside a designated MPA by my calculation. The published figure is about 37%. Either way, this is above the 30% area threshold.









The national figure hides a lot of variation between regions, so read the chart alongside the map.
Change over time. Scotland’s Marine Assessment 2020 reports that the network covered about 22% of Scotland’s seas in 2018, rising to 37% after new designations in 2020. I have not rebuilt that time series from boundaries, so the trend arrow rests on the published figures.
Checks. My figure (229,228 km², 36.9%) is within 0.5% of the published 228,121 km² (36.9%). Counting all SACs and SPAs, rather than only those flagged as part of the MPA network, changed the total by less than 50 km², so the result is not sensitive to that choice.

title: MPA coverage and 30x30
section: Designated is not the same as effectively managed
text:
Designated is not the same as effectively managed

Designation sets out what a site protects and why.
Management measures (for example, fisheries restrictions) decide whether activities that could damage protected features are actually controlled. Measures for some inshore MPAs and Priority Marine Features have been the subject of recent Scottish Government consultation.
Condition monitoring shows whether protected features are improving, stable, or declining.

So this indicator answers “how much is designated?” but not “how much is protected well enough to make a difference?”. An honest GBF Target 3 assessment needs all three layers.

title: MPA coverage and 30x30
text:
Confidence
Medium overall. High for the area calculation. The boundaries are official, and my figure can be checked against the published total. Low for what it says about protection in practice, for the reasons above.

title: MPA coverage and 30x30
text:
Limitations

Area only: says nothing about how well sites represent habitats, how they connect, or what condition they are in.
My total depends on which site types and which sea boundary are included, so it may differ slightly from official figures.
Historic MPAs, the Demonstration and Research MPA, and other area-based measures (OECMs) are not included.
Boundaries are simplified for the web map. Areas are calculated on the full-resolution boundaries.

title: Sea temperature
text:
What this measures
Near-surface sea temperature, sampled weekly by boat at the Scottish Coastal Observatory’s two long-term ecosystem monitoring sites:

Stonehaven, about 3 km off the Aberdeenshire coast in the North Sea, sampled since 1997.
Loch Ewe, a sea loch in Wester Ross on the Atlantic-influenced west coast, sampled since 1999.

I express each month as an anomaly: how much warmer or cooler it was than the 1999 to 2020 average for that calendar month. Near-surface samples at Loch Ewe begin in mid-2002, so its usable series and baseline effectively start in 2003. This removes the seasonal cycle so that years can be compared fairly.

title: Sea temperature
text:
Why it matters
Temperature shapes almost everything else in a marine ecosystem: plankton timing, fish distribution, seabird food supply, and the spread of warm-water species. This is a context indicator. It has no “good” or “bad” direction on its own, but it helps explain change in the biological indicators on this site.

Ordinary least squares on annual mean anomalies. Positive residual autocorrelation means the true uncertainty is somewhat wider than the interval shown.








Stonehaven: +0.02°C per decade (95% CI -0.16 to +0.20), an interval that includes zero.
Loch Ewe: -0.16°C per decade (95% CI -0.45 to +0.13), an interval that includes zero.
Over roughly two decades, year-to-year variability is large compared with the long-term trend, so a single unusually warm or cold year can move the fitted line. That is why I report the confidence interval and not just the slope.

Why no clear trend?
This does not mean Scottish seas are not warming. It is a question of time window:

Over the long term, Scottish waters (coastal and oceanic) have warmed by about 0.05 to 0.07°C per decade over 1870 to 2016, with faster warming over the most recent 30 years of that period (Scotland’s Marine Assessment 2020).
Over the shorter, more recent window these two sites cover, Scotland’s Marine Assessment 2020 also reports no significant linear trend in the most recent decade. It links a cold anomaly in the waters west of Scotland to strong ocean heat loss from the winter of 2013 to 2014.
Two sites over about 20 years cannot separate a long-term trend from multi-decadal natural variability in the North Atlantic.

So the honest reading is: no detectable trend at these two sites over 1997 to 2020, consistent with the published regional picture, and not evidence against long-term warming. Adding the 2021 onwards data, once published, would be the most useful next step.

title: Sea temperature
text:
Confidence
Medium. These are carefully quality-controlled observations from fixed sites with a consistent method. But:

They are two points, not a picture of all Scottish seas.
Weekly sampling can miss short events such as marine heatwaves.
The published record currently ends in 2020, so the most recent years are not included.

title: Sea temperature
text:
Limitations

The record is about 20 years long. That is short for separating a long-term trend from natural variability such as the North Atlantic Oscillation.
Months with missing visits make monthly means less certain. Years with fewer than 9 months of data are excluded from the annual series, which drops 2020 at Stonehaven.
Near-surface means the shallowest sample on each visit, up to 5 m. Bottom water can behave differently, especially at Stonehaven, where the water column stratifies in summer.
Loch Ewe is a sheltered sea loch, so it is not fully representative of open west-coast waters.

title: Harbour and grey seals
text:
What this measures
The number of harbour seals and grey seals counted hauled out on land during the harbour seal moult in August, from helicopter surveys by the Sea Mammal Research Unit (SMRU). The whole Scottish coastline is surveyed roughly every five years. Counts are reported for Scotland’s seven Seal Management Units (SMUs).
A count is not a population estimate. Many seals are at sea during any survey. Comparing counts across years works because surveys follow a consistent method at the same time of year.

title: Harbour and grey seals
text:
Why it matters
Both species are protected under the Marine (Scotland) Act 2010 and are features of Special Areas of Conservation. Harbour seals in particular have declined sharply in parts of Scotland since the early 2000s, and the causes are not fully understood. Seal counts feed into OSPAR and UK Marine Strategy assessments of marine mammals.

title: Harbour and grey seals
text:
Trend and status
The 2021 to 2025 census counted 19,978 harbour seals, the lowest Scottish total since the first full census in 1996-97 and 26% below 2016-19. It counted 16,042 grey seals in August, 37% below 2016-19.


















Grey seals need extra care. August counts capture grey seals hauled out in summer, which is not the main way their population is monitored (that is through pup production in autumn). The report notes that the low 2021-25 grey seal total is driven mainly by a very low 2025 count in Orkney, so one survey has a big influence.

title: Harbour and grey seals
text:
Confidence
High. These are systematic, repeated national surveys by a specialist team using consistent methods, and the declines are large relative to survey uncertainty in most units. Confidence is lower for:

Grey seals in August, as above.
Single-year counts in any one area, which can be affected by weather and disturbance on the survey day.

title: Harbour and grey seals
text:
Limitations

Counts are a minimum, not a population size. The report scales the latest counts to population estimates with wide confidence intervals.
Census periods span several years, so the “midpoint” on the charts is a simplification.
Survey methods changed over time (for example, the move to thermal imaging), which the report describes.
The data describe change, not its causes. SCOS and SMRU continue to investigate potential drivers of harbour seal decline.
